The Bottleneck Is Retrieval, Not Reading: Diagnosing Evidence-Based Generation with RAG for Long Context Question Answering

Debopriyo Banerjee    Owais Aijaz    Ahmer Tabassum    Zhuohan Xie Affiliation: MBZUAI {deb.ban89, vesko.st}@gmail.com preslav.nakov@mbzuai.ac.ae  Project     Code    Preslav Nakov Affiliation: MBZUAI {deb.ban89, vesko.st}@gmail.com preslav.nakov@mbzuai.ac.ae  Project     Code    Veselin Stoyanov Affiliation: MBZUAI {deb.ban89, vesko.st}@gmail.com preslav.nakov@mbzuai.ac.ae  Project     Code Affiliation: Inception42
Abstract

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is the dominant paradigm for grounding large language models in external corpora, but its similarity-driven, chunked pipeline has structural blind spots: it cannot anticipate which passages a question requires and discards document-level context that resolves cross-passage references. We introduce evidence-based generation (EBG), requiring models to return an answer with line-level citations, and a joint Ans+Evid metric that scores correctness and grounding simultaneously. We reformulate two corpora into evidence-grounded multi-document QA benchmarks - MultiHop-RAG and QASPER-MP, a multi-paper adaptation of QASPER with realistic short paper cues, and pair them with a controlled synthetic two-hop haystack and an evidence-augmented NoLiMa spanning 10K–1M characters. Across ten proprietary frontier and three open-weight LLMs, EBG isolates two RAG limitations that long-context models avoid: similarity retrieval surfaces any relevant chunk far more reliably than all required chunks for multi-fact queries, and chunking destroys document meta-information needed to resolve identity-bearing queries. EBG also exposes grounding failures invisible to answer-only evaluation, including incomplete citations in two-needle settings and a widening gap between Ans and Ans+Evid when context contradicts parametric knowledge. Data and code are available at https://github.com/debobanerjee/LC-EBG.

1 Introduction

Large Language Models (LLMs) can rapidly process large text volumes to identify information relevant to a query. This capability suits applications such as legal discovery, medical analysis, financial due diligence, literature review, etc., which require synthesis from large document collections.

The predominant paradigm for grounding LLM outputs in external knowledge is retrieval-augmented generation (Lewis et al., 2020, RAG;), which retrieves passages via embedding similarity and conditions the generator on those passages alone. While effective for single-fact lookups, this design has several structural limitations. First, each retrieved chunk is stripped of its surrounding context: the model cannot see where a paragraph falls within a document or how it relates to neighboring sections. Second, document-level metadata (authorship, date, section hierarchy) is typically lost during chunking. Third, and most critically, similarity-based retrieval cannot anticipate which combination of passages will be needed for questions requiring integration across multiple locations. This is particularly acute for multi-hop questions, where the answer depends on chaining facts that may appear in distant, semantically dissimilar passages (Karpukhin et al., 2020; Li et al., 2024).

Our goal in this paper is not to advocate replacing RAG with long-context (LC) models outright, but to make these structural limitations measurable. RAG systems are typically evaluated on answer correctness alone, which conflates two very different failure modes: the retriever fails to surface the right passages, or the reader fails to use them. To separate the two, we propose evidence-based generation (EBG), a paradigm where the model must produce both an answer and explicit references to the input lines that support it. EBG inherits RAG’s built-in verifiability (Lewis et al., 2020), but extends it to long-context settings where the model is given the full document neighborhood and must select its own evidence. The joint Ans+Evid metric pinpoints where a pipeline breaks: in retrieval, in grounding, or in reading. Recent work shows LC models can match or exceed RAG accuracy given sufficient context (Li et al., 2024; Laitenberger et al., 2025), but without provenance these comparisons are inconclusive; EBG closes that gap.

We make the following contributions:

  • •

    EBG framework. We define the evidence-based generation task and a joint Ans+Evid metric, and evaluate ten proprietary frontier and three open-weight LLMs under matched LC and RAG conditions across 10K–1M character contexts.

  • •

    Evidence-grounded benchmarks. We reformulate two corpora into evidence-grounded multi-document QA benchmarks—a re-instrumented MultiHop-RAG with line-level evidence labels, and QASPER-MP, a multi-paper QASPER adaptation with realistic paper cues, and pair them with a controlled two-hop synthetic haystack and an evidence-augmented NoLiMa. The first two stress retrieval; the last two stress long-context reading.

  • •

    Characterizing RAG’s limitations. Using EBG, we isolate two failure modes of similarity-based RAG that LC sidesteps: (i) retrieval recovers any relevant chunk far more reliably than all required chunks for multi-fact queries, and (ii) chunking discards document meta-information that identity-bearing queries depend on. On MultiHop-RAG, the retrieval ceiling at realistic top-k budgets, not the reader, is the binding constraint.

  • •

    Diagnostic analysis of LC grounding. Beyond the RAG comparison, EBG reveals that citation acts as a reasoning scaffold, that models cite incomplete evidence in two-needle settings, and that grounding degrades sharply when in-context evidence contradicts parametric knowledge.

2 Related Work

2.1 Long-Context Language Models

Advances in transformer architectures have expanded context windows from thousands to hundreds of thousands of tokens through improved positional encoding such as ALiBi (Press et al., 2022), RoPE extensions (Su et al., 2024), and memory-augmented attention (Wu et al., 2022). Training data matters equally, as pretraining corpora rarely contain long-range dependencies; Zhuang et al. (2025) construct data with long-distance references encouraging use of distant context. Yet larger windows do not automatically yield better reasoning. Du et al. (2025) show accuracy degrades with context length even under perfect retrieval, suggesting a processing bottleneck. Similarly, Liu et al. (2024) show performance drops when information appears mid-input rather than at boundaries.

2.2 Evaluating Long-Context Reasoning

Early long-context evaluations relied on needle-in-a-haystack tests (Kamradt, 2024), which mainly measure retrieval of planted information rather than reasoning. Subsequent work argues that such evaluations set the bar too low, since strong performance often reflects shallow heuristics rather than genuine understanding (Liu et al., 2024; Schuster et al., 2025; Modarressi et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2024; Yen et al., 2025). Recent benchmarks shift toward more demanding evaluations: ∞\inftyBench (Zhang et al., 2024) studies degradation beyond 100K characters, HELMET (Yen et al., 2025) shows that benchmark choice substantially alters rankings, and NoLiMa (Modarressi et al., 2025) removes lexical shortcuts by requiring semantic matching between queries and evidence. However, these benchmarks still score models on final answers alone, leaving open whether correct answers stem from actual use of relevant context or from priors, surface cues, or chance. Unlike these answer-only benchmarks, our work focuses on grounding by requiring models to return both answers and supporting input lines, distinguishing genuine reasoning from lucky guessing and enabling a more faithful assessment of whether models use long contexts effectively and reliably.

2.3 Retrieval-Augmented Generation

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) (Lewis et al., 2020) remains the dominant approach for grounding LLMs in external knowledge. Built on dense retrieval (Karpukhin et al., 2020) and multi-passage readers such as Fusion-in-Decoder (Izacard and Grave, 2021), RAG provides provenance by construction since retrieved passages serve as evidence. Recent work revisits RAG alongside long-context models, highlighting a trade-off between the two paradigms (Li et al., 2024; Laitenberger et al., 2025): long-context prompting generally improves accuracy but at substantially higher cost, motivating hybrid systems that route queries by difficulty (Li et al., 2024). Controlled comparisons also show well-tuned single-stage RAG can match elaborate multi-stage pipelines once token budgets are equalized (Laitenberger et al., 2025), while adaptive retrieval and self-reflection improve factuality and citation quality (Asai et al., 2024). Existing work primarily evaluates these approaches on accuracy or efficiency. We instead focus on grounding, distinguishing whether evidence was available from whether the model actually used it.

3 Evidence-based Generation (EBG)

We formalize evidence-based generation (EBG) as a grounded question-answering paradigm that extends standard answer-only evaluation by requiring models to generate both answers and explicit citations to the supporting input evidence.

3.1 Answer-only vs Evidence-based Generation

Existing long-context evaluations, including NoLiMa (Modarressi et al., 2025), use answer-only evaluation, omitting the grounding needed to validate model reasoning. EBG extends this formulation by requiring models to generate both explicit evidence references to supporting input lines and the final answer, yielding a stricter evaluation setting in which correctness depends on both accurate reasoning and faithful grounding.

To illustrate the distinction, consider a haystack containing the sentence “Then Stuart mentioned that he has been vegan for years.” at line 1,284 and the question “Which character cannot eat Brandade?” - a two-hop query requiring the inference that Brandade contains fish and is therefore incompatible with veganism. The answer-only and EBG settings differ in both the system instruction and the required output format.

Under answer-only evaluation, the response ‘‘Stuart’’ is simply marked correct. But under EBG, the same response is evaluated using three complementary metrics: answer accuracy (Ans), evidence accuracy (Evid), and their conjunction (Ans+Evid). While Ans preserves standard answer correctness, Ans+Evid additionally requires the model to cite the supporting evidence at line 1,284. Together, these metrics separate answer correctness from evidence-grounded correctness.

This decomposition exposes silent failures hidden by answer-only evaluation: a model may arrive at the correct answer while citing irrelevant lines, or retrieve the correct evidence while producing the wrong answer. The joint Ans+Evid metric therefore serves as the strictest measure of evidence-based reasoning, requiring both accurate reasoning and faithful grounding.

We also evaluate vanilla Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, following Modarressi et al. (2025), and a CoT-based EBG prompting variant. The prompt templates are in Appendix A.

3.2 RAG under EBG

In this work, we evaluate RAG systems within the EBG framework by requiring models to not only answer using retrieved chunks, but also to explicitly cite the supporting evidence. This yields two RAG variants:

  • •

    Answer-only RAG: Standard formulation requiring answer correctness only.

  • •

    Answer + Evidence RAG: EBG formulation requiring correct answer and correct citation.

This unified view allows us to decompose end-to-end performance into two factors:

  • •

    Evidence availability: whether the retriever surfaces the relevant needle(s) (Hit@k),

  • •

    Evidence utilization: whether the model correctly uses and cites the retrieved evidence (long-context accuracy).

Overall, our formulation shows that RAG and EBG are not competing paradigms but complementary components: retrieval determines what evidence is available, while EBG determines whether that evidence is correctly used and cited.

4 Benchmarks

To systematically evaluate EBG and RAG under EBG, we construct four complementary benchmarks: a fully synthetic benchmark, an evidence-augmented version of NoLiMa, MultiHop-RAG, and QASPER-MP (an adapted version of QASPER). Together, they evaluate EBG under both controlled synthetic settings and realistic long-context scenarios.

4.1 Synthetic Dataset

The synthetic benchmark provides precise control over haystack content and evidence placement. It consists of a distractor fact pool, a curated needle set, and a haystack generation procedure. This controlled construction allows us to vary context length independently of task difficulty while retaining exact ground-truth evidence locations.

Distractor fact pool.

We construct a fixed pool of 66,834 unique single-sentence facts using iterative LLM prompting followed by deduplication, ensuring that distractors are not confusable with inserted needles. The large pool also limits repeated distractors across independently generated trials and provides sufficient diversity for constructing long haystacks.

Needle set.

We manually curate 10 two-hop needles, each containing: i) two atomic supporting facts, ii) a compositional question requiring both facts, and iii) accepted answer surface forms. The needles span relations such as company–product associations, founder–specialty links, and birthplace lookups. By requiring composition across two independently placed facts, the benchmark tests both evidence retrieval and integration rather than simple single-fact recall.

Haystack assembly.

For a target length LL, distractor facts are shuffled and accumulated until reaching LL characters, after which the two needle facts are inserted at independently sampled positions and recorded as gold evidence. Haystacks are formatted as line-numbered i: fact entries and evaluated under the EBG prompt template (§ A). Each trial uses a newly generated haystack and a uniformly sampled needle. Consequently, performance differences cannot be attributed to a fixed ordering of distractors or evidence positions. Appendix B.1 provides a representative example.

Sanity check.

At L=10​KL{=}10\text{K} (≈2​K{\approx}2\text{K} tokens), all evaluated frontier models achieve at least 0.980.98 joint Ans+Evid accuracy over N=100N{=}100 trials, confirming that the inserted needles are unambiguous and readily solvable when context length is modest. Any degradation at larger LL therefore reflects failures in long-context evidence retrieval or integration rather than intrinsic task ambiguity. This makes the synthetic benchmark a controlled probe of how model reliability changes as relevant evidence becomes increasingly sparse within the surrounding context.

4.2 NoLiMa-based Dataset

We adapt the NoLiMa haystack construction procedure to create long-context inputs ranging from L=10​KL{=}10\text{K} to 1​M1\text{M} characters and require models to both answer questions and cite supporting needles as evidence. This converts NoLiMa from an answer-only benchmark into an evidence-grounded evaluation that tests whether models truly use the provided context.

Needle set.

We use the original single-needle (SN) setting from NoLiMa (Modarressi et al., 2025), specifically the 0402 and 0405 needle groups with both default and inverse variants under the commonsense category. Each needle contains a character name and a single factual attribute, and supports both one-hop and two-hop questions.

We further introduce a two-needle (TN) setting, in which the explicit secondary needle is consistent with world knowledge, and a contradictory two-needle (CTN) variant, in which it conflicts with world knowledge. Appendix C.1 provides additional details and templates for SN, TN, and CTN settings.

Haystack assembly.

We adopt the random book generation procedure from NoLiMa (Modarressi et al., 2025) to construct haystacks ranging from 10K to 1M characters (10K–50K in 10K increments and 100K–1M in 100K increments), generating three random books B1c,B2c,B3c{B^{c}_{1},B^{c}_{2},B^{c}_{3}} for each context length cc. Because tokenization is model-dependent, we vary input length in characters rather than tokens. Each haystack is split into line-indexed entries using the ‘\n’ delimiter. In the single-needle setting, the needle is inserted at one of four normalized depths: 0, 0.33, 0.67, or 1.0. In the two-needle setting, the primary needle is fixed at depth 0.5, while the secondary needle is inserted at one of the same four depths.

4.3 Multi-document QA Datasets

To stress the retrieval pipeline on the dimensions it is meant to handle, we reformulate two existing corpora into evidence-grounded multi-document question answering (QA) benchmarks. Both are designed to make RAG’s retrieval-vs.-reading split observable: gold evidence is labeled at the line (sentence or paragraph) level, so the same scoring code works for LC and any retriever-ordered context.

MultiHop-RAG (Tang and Yang, 2024).

The official release contains 609 news articles (4.6M characters, 1.2M tokens with the cl100k_base tokenizer) and 2,556 queries in four templated types: inference, comparison, temporal, and null_query (unanswerable). Each non-null query carries an evidence_list of 2–4 gold facts, each consisting of a source article title and an exact textual span. Removing the 301 null_query items leaves 2,255 usable queries; for the pilot reported in this paper, we uniformly sample 50 queries (seed 0), naturally stratified across the three answerable types (ninf=13n_{\text{inf}}{=}13, ncomp=21n_{\text{comp}}{=}21, ntemp=16n_{\text{temp}}{=}16).

For the LC condition, we construct an oracle-containing per-query mini-haystack comprising every gold-evidence article plus 20 distractor articles sampled from the remainder of the corpus. The articles are concatenated in random order and split into sentence-per-line entries, producing contexts of approximately 241K characters on average. For the RAG condition, we perform open-corpus retrieval over the full 609-article corpus: we divide the corpus into 256-token sliding windows (6,296 chunks), embed the chunks with text-embedding-3-large, and rank them by cosine similarity to produce top-KK contexts for K∈{4,10,25,50,100,200}K\in\{4,10,25,50,100,200\}.

The two conditions are therefore not pool-matched: LC evaluates reading and evidence utilization when all gold source articles are guaranteed present, whereas RAG must first retrieve the required evidence from the full corpus. Accordingly, this experiment diagnoses the contribution of open-corpus retrieval failures to end-to-end performance; it is not a direct LC–RAG comparison under identical candidate pools. In both conditions, gold facts are re-mapped to line numbers inside the assembled context; in RAG, a gold fact that is not retrieved has no corresponding gold line. Appendix D reports the corresponding retrieval ceilings (Hits@kk for any vs. all gold facts) and reproduces the answer-only RAG baselines from the original paper.

QASPER-MP.

QASPER (Dasigi et al., 2021) contains 5,049 information-seeking questions over 1,585 NLP papers, each annotated by domain experts with paragraph-level evidence and a short free-form or extractive answer (including Unanswerable). The original task is single-document and, therefore, does not exercise the retrieval pipeline.

We construct QASPER-MP (multi-paper) by pairing each gold paper with ten distractor papers sampled from the QASPER pool, yielding an 11-paper haystack per query, and rewrite every question to include a realistic paper cue - in ∼\sim50% of cases a first-author surname (e.g., “Smith et al.”), and otherwise a 2–3 word verbatim title fragment - split by a hash of the question id. This forces the system to resolve document identity from a realistic cue rather than the full paper title. The task jointly tests document identification, evidence localization, and answer generation. Since distractors come from the same NLP-paper collection, they provide domain-matched context. A successful system must identify the relevant paper and supporting paragraph(s) before answering, while retaining QASPER’s expert-annotated answers and evidence.

For LC, papers are serialized in an XML-like format that preserves titles, abstracts, and section structure (<paper>, <title>, <abstract>, <section>); paragraphs are line-numbered, and the same paragraph-level gold labels are used for evidence scoring. For RAG, we evaluate both a flat variant (concatenate the top-KK retrieved paragraphs in rank order) and a structured variant that re-emits the surrounding <paper>/<title>/<abstract> scaffolding and inserts “...” markers for discontinuities, so that retrieved fragments retain their document provenance.

We evaluate QASPER-MP at two scales. For proprietary models, we conduct a pilot on N=50N{=}50 queries, comprising 38 answerable and 12 unanswerable examples. For open-weight models, we expand the evaluation to N=200N{=}200 queries, providing broader benchmark coverage and a more stable estimate of aggregate performance. Because the proprietary-model results are based on the smaller pilot, comparisons across the two model groups should be interpreted with the corresponding difference in sampling uncertainty in mind. Construction details, sampling procedures, prompts, and the LLM-judge protocol are provided in Appendix E.

5 Experiments

We organize our experiments around four research questions:

  • •

    RQ1. What are the practical limitations of RAG, and can long-context EBG address them?

  • •

    RQ2. Does requiring models to explicitly cite evidence improve answer accuracy?

  • •

    RQ3. Can models correctly cite evidence lines even in a two-needle setting?

  • •

    RQ4. Can models remain context-faithful even when evidence contradicts their built-in knowledge?

5.1 Experimental Setup

We evaluate 10 state-of-the-art proprietary models from three major providers across different experiments: GPT-4o, GPT-4.1, o3-mini, GPT-5, GPT-5.5, Sonnet-4, Sonnet-4.5, Opus-4.6, Gemini-2.5-Fl, and Gemini-3-Fl. Additionally we evaluate three open-weight models served through Fireworks.ai11 1 https://fireworks.ai/  -  GPT-OSS-120B, GLM-5.2, and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B (or Nemo-3.5-L in short) - to test whether our findings hold beyond proprietary systems. We evaluate evidence-based generation (EBG) under both long-context (LC) and RAG settings. Prompt templates for the answer-only and EBG conditions are provided in Appendix A.

5.1.1 Multi-document QA setup.

For RQ1, we use two multi-document QA datasets - MultiHop-RAG and QASPER-MP. Construction details, retrieval variants, and the LLM-judge protocol are in Appendices D and E.

5.1.2 EBG Setup

Synthetic Dataset.

We sweep context lengths from 10K to 1M characters. For each length, we run N=100N{=}100 trials: each trial draws a fresh distractor haystack and samples one needle uniformly from the 10 curated two-hop needles. Here we apply the answer-only and EBG prompts and report Ans*, Ans, Evid, and Ans+Evid accuracies. A sanity check at L=10​KL{=}10\text{K} confirms all models achieve ≥0.98{\geq}0.98 joint accuracy, establishing that degradation at longer lengths reflects context handling rather than needle ambiguity. This setup addresses RQ2 and RQ3; there are no contradictory needles, so RQ4 is not evaluated here.

NoLiMa-based Dataset.

Under the NoLiMa setting, we use B1cB^{c}_{1} as the haystack source across all context lengths to maintain a controlled evaluation setup. We use the T01 test variant throughout, as it provides exactly one input argument for the one-hop question and one for the two-hop question associated with each needle. This enables a consistent comparison between direct retrieval and commonsense composition while holding the underlying needle fixed. For example, for 0405, the one-hop question is instantiated with fish-based meals, whereas the two-hop question uses Brandade; similarly, 0402 uses milk and a cappuccino, respectively. We test two characters, Yuki and Stuart, at the insertion depths defined in § 4.2, yielding 16 needle-placement conditions per context length per model (4 needles ×\times 4 depths).

We evaluate three settings: single-needle (one-hop and two-hop, addressing RQ2), two-needle (two-hop with explicit secondary evidence, addressing RQ3), and contradictory two-needle (CTN, addressing RQ4). Results are reported separately for one-hop and two-hop questions and averaged across the corresponding conditions.

5.1.3 NoLiMa-based RAG Setup

We compare long-context LC and RAG on the NoLiMa-based dataset under RQ1 (Appendix G). We first analyze RAG retrieval performance for the single-needle and two-needle settings using one-hop and two-hop questions, examining how the retrieval depth required for full evidence coverage changes with haystack length and reasoning complexity. After needle insertion, each haystack line is embedded using OpenAI’s text-embedding-3-small model and ranked by cosine similarity to the query.

We then compare RAG and LC under the same EBG prompting, reporting Ans accuracy. Since RAG contexts can be smaller than their source haystacks, we use matched character budgets. For each haystack length, we identify the minimum top-kk providing full evidence coverage, compute its character count, and match it to the closest available LC context length. Table 15 summarizes this mapping. For example, full-coverage retrieval from the 1M-character haystack in the two-needle setting requires 920 vectors (217,152 characters) and is matched to the 200K LC condition. This approximately controls for the amount of text presented to the model and isolates retrieval-ranked versus long-context inputs under comparable budgets.

5.2 Results

We report results organized by the research questions introduced in § 5.

RQ1: LC-EBG addresses two RAG limitations.

On MultiHop-RAG, queries require 2–4 evidence facts spread across distinct articles, so faithful answering requires the retriever to surface all required facts within its top-kk budget. For this benchmark, the two conditions use different evidence-access regimes: open-corpus RAG searches 6,296 chunks constructed from all 609 articles, whereas the oracle-containing LC condition receives every gold-evidence article plus 20 distractor articles. The conditions are therefore not pool-matched; this comparison diagnoses the cost of open-corpus retrieval relative to reading when the gold source articles are guaranteed to be available.

We first reproduce the answer-only RAG baselines from the original benchmark under our pipeline (text-embedding-3-large + 256-token windows; Appendix D) and measure annotated-gold retrieval coverage directly. At k=10k{=}10, the retriever covers any gold fact for 82%82\% of queries but covers all gold facts for only 19%19\% (and just 8%8\% on inference queries). This all-vs-any gap exposes a limitation of the evaluated similarity-retrieval setup: it often retrieves some relevant evidence but fails to recover the complete evidence set required for multi-fact queries within a practical top-kk budget. When the gold annotations are exhaustive and every annotated fact is necessary, all-gold coverage bounds the faithfully grounded performance of the downstream RAG reader. The reader results corroborate this limitation (Appendix D.5, Table 6).

Under EBG prompting at k=10k{=}10, open-corpus RAG achieves Ans accuracies of 60/48/44%60/48/44\% for GPT-5, Sonnet-4.5, and Gemini-3-Fl, respectively, whereas the oracle-containing LC-EBG condition achieves 86/82/78%86/82/78\% on the same queries. The resulting 2626–3434 pp gap includes the cost of retrieving the required evidence from the full corpus and should not be interpreted as a pool-matched estimate of an intrinsic LC–RAG difference. The gap remains at k=200k{=}200, where the open-corpus RAG context approaches the size of the LC haystack despite comparable context sizes, but its Ans accuracy remains lower for all three models. Under answer-only prompting, open-corpus RAG at k=200k{=}200 reaches parity with the oracle-containing LC condition only for Sonnet-4.5 (68%68\% vs. 68%68\%).

Consistent with this, our NoLiMa-based RAG analysis (Table 13) shows that retrieval costs scale sharply with reasoning complexity and haystack length. While one-hop full coverage remains relatively efficient, two-hop retrieval grows from 1.9K retrieved characters at 10K context to over 202K at 1M context, effectively pushing RAG toward brute-force long-context processing without guaranteeing complete evidence recovery.

On QASPER-MP, the query refers to a paper by an author or short title cue; answering requires document-level identity, not just topical fragments. This exposes a second limitation of RAG: chunk-level similarity retrieval struggles with document identity and provenance when queries refer indirectly to a source. Table 1 reports answerable-subset judge scores for the pool-matched comparison, where LC-EBG and RAG use the same 11-paper pool. LC-EBG exceeds the best pool-matched RAG variant for all five frontier models by +0.05+0.05 to +0.13+0.13 judge points. Aggregate scores look tied only because RAG over-refuses on missed retrievals (2424–40%40\% on answerable queries vs. 1313–18%18\% for LC-EBG), accidentally matching QASPER’s Unanswerable gold label on the 24% of pilot questions for which it is correct. Under the open-corpus condition (flat_full@10), all-needles coverage drops to 48%, and the judge-score gap relative to LC is 5–13 points (Appendix E).

Across both datasets, retrieval is a major error source despite different evidence-access regimes: MultiHop-RAG compares open-corpus RAG with oracle-containing LC, whereas QASPER-MP uses a pool-matched 11-paper comparison. This pattern persists for three open-weight readers on n=200n{=}200 queries, with LC exceeding RAG by +13+13 to +36+36 pp in EBG Ans accuracy on MultiHop-RAG and by +0.07+0.07 to +0.24+0.24 answerable-subset judge points on QASPER-MP, alongside a large residual grounding gap (Appendices D.7 and E.6).

RQ2: Citation improves answer accuracy.

On the synthetic benchmark (Fig. 4(a), Appendix F.1), all three frontier models - GPT-5, Claude Sonnet-4.5, and Gemini-3-Flash - approach ceiling answer accuracy under both prompting conditions (answer-only and EBG). GPT-5 and Gemini-3-Flash maintain ≥98%\geq 98\% accuracy across all tested context lengths, while Sonnet-4.5 remains within the 9393–100%100\% range up to 700K characters. Consequently, the synthetic dataset shows no measurable citation-as-scaffold effect on answer accuracy: Ans∗ and Ans remain within sampling noise across all cells, including at the longest contexts. This does not refute RQ2 but reflects the controlled benchmark design: lexically dissimilar distractors make the two-hop facts relatively easy to isolate, leaving little headroom for EBG’s benefits.

A different pattern emerges on the more challenging NoLiMa-based LC benchmark (Fig. 1), where the scaffolding effect becomes apparent under long-context stress. Sonnet and Gemini models gain between +9+9 and +19+19 pp from EBG prompting across context lengths from 300K to 900K. Among open-weight models, the smaller Nemo-3.5-L improves by +3+3 to +12+12 pp, while GLM-5.2 reaches a maximum gain of +16+16 pp at 700K; in contrast, GPT-OSS-120B shows no benefit. Taken together, the contrast between the synthetic and NoLiMa settings suggests that scaffolding is most useful when long-context retrieval is sufficiently challenging, while its effectiveness remains model-dependent and may not simply scale with model capacity.

RQ3: Asymmetric Retrieval Behavior.

As shown in Fig. 2, recovery of the two evidence types varies substantially across models. Gemini-3-Fl and GPT-5 achieve near-perfect and balanced citation of both the primary and secondary needles (99.5/99.8% and 95.1/98.6%, respectively). Gemini-2.5-Fl also performs relatively well, but exhibits an inversion, with secondary-needle citation exceeding primary-needle citation (80.8% vs. 67.4%). A similar, more pronounced inversion appears for o3-mini (88.4% vs. 54.9%). These cases suggest that successful recovery of one evidence type does not necessarily imply comparable recovery of the other.

This asymmetry reverses for several other models, where primary-needle recovery substantially exceeds secondary-needle recovery. GPT-4.1, GPT-4o, and the Sonnet models exhibit this pattern, with the largest disparities observed for GPT-4o (71.3% vs. 20.9%) and Sonnet-4.5 (64.6% vs. 21.4%). This disparity indicates that retrieving the primary evidence does not guarantee successful attribution of the complementary evidence required for the task. Moreover, primary-needle citation itself remains imperfect, showing that retrieval failures extend beyond the secondary signal alone.

The open-weight models show substantial variation in retrieval. GLM-5.2 achieves balanced recovery (78.5% primary and 85.2% secondary), whereas GPT-OSS-120B records lower rates for both needles (26.1% and 29.4%). Nemo-3.5-L performs poorly on both (11.8% and 6.5%), indicating broader retrieval limitation rather than directional asymmetry. Overall, multi-evidence retrieval varies across models and evidence types, reinforcing model-dependent patterns as in RQ1.

RQ4: CTN amplifies failure.

Performance generally declines under contradiction, with substantial variation across models (Fig. 3); answer accuracy is reported separately in Figure 6. GPT-5 and Gemini-3-Fl remain relatively context-faithful, preserving high answer accuracy, though their Ans+Evid still drops, indicating greater sensitivity of evidence grounding to contradiction. In contrast, GPT-4.1, GPT-4o, and the Sonnet variants show sharper declines, particularly in Ans+Evid, suggesting they can recover the expected answer while failing to reconcile contradictory evidence.

CTN robustness is also uneven among open-weight models. GLM-5.2 is notably resilient: Ans decreases only from 79% to 72%, while Ans+Evid changes from 73% to 70%, largely preserving the small gap between the two metrics. By contrast, GPT-OSS-120B and Nemo-3.5-L start from substantially weaker TN baselines: the former falls from 28/8% (Ans/Ans+Evid) to 8/5% under CTN, and the latter from 12/6% to 5/4%. These models therefore already struggle to extract and ground answers under TN, with CTN further compounding this weakness.

Overall, Ans+Evid is generally more vulnerable to CTN than Ans, showing that resolving contradiction while grounding the answer in supplied evidence is harder than producing the correct answer itself. The widening Ans–Ans+Evid gap highlights a common failure mode: models reach the expected answer without faithfully using the context that should justify it, even when answers remain correct. See Appendix F.4 for more details.

6 Conclusion and Future Work

We introduced evidence-based generation (EBG), a framework that requires models to produce both an answer and line-level citations, together with a joint Ans+Evid metric that measures correctness and grounding simultaneously. By separating retrieval from evidence-grounded reasoning, EBG exposes failures obscured by answer-only evaluation. We evaluate these failures using evidence-grounded versions of MultiHop-RAG and QASPER-MP, a controlled synthetic two-hop haystack, and an evidence-augmented NoLiMa spanning 10K–1M characters. This evaluation suite spans both realistic and controlled settings, allowing retrieval, reasoning, and grounding errors to be examined under complementary conditions.

Across ten proprietary frontier and three open-weight LLMs, EBG reveals two key RAG limitations: (i) similarity retrieval finds any relevant chunk more reliably than all evidence required for multi-fact queries, imposing a retrieval ceiling at realistic top-kk budgets; and (ii) chunking can discard document-level meta-information needed by identity-bearing queries, causing RAG to over-refuse on retrieval misses. EBG further exposes grounding failures hidden by answer-only metrics: models often cite incomplete evidence, and the gap between answer and joint accuracy widens when in-context evidence conflicts with parametric knowledge. These findings show that correct answers alone can substantially overstate a model’s ability to faithfully use long-context evidence. They also highlight evidence attribution as a useful diagnostic for distinguishing retrieval limitations from downstream reasoning failures. Consequently, EBG provides a more informative basis for comparing RAG and long-context systems than evaluations that collapse retrieval, reasoning, and attribution into answer accuracy alone.

These results do not imply that “LC replaces RAG”; rather, LC and RAG exhibit distinct failure modes that EBG helps localize, motivating evaluations that measure both answer accuracy and evidence fidelity. The appropriate architecture may therefore depend not only on answer quality, but also on which sources of failure are acceptable for a given task and context regime. Future work includes scaling EBG to the full benchmarks and testing document-aware chunking. Richer evidence attribution and the observed reasoning benefits of evidence generation also motivate investigating grounding objectives as part of model training.

Limitations

Our evaluation focuses on synthetic and semi-synthetic long-context benchmarks designed to isolate grounding and evidence attribution behavior under controlled conditions. While these settings enable precise analysis, they do not capture the full complexity of real-world domains such as legal, scientific, or medical reasoning. In addition, our evidence metric operates at the line level and therefore measures coarse-grained provenance rather than fine-grained span-level attribution. The benchmarks also assume that the reference evidence is sufficiently complete and unambiguous, whereas real-world questions may admit multiple valid evidence sets or interpretations.

Our RAG analysis estimates end-to-end performance through a decomposition of retrieval and long-context accuracy rather than exhaustive evaluation of full production RAG pipelines across all configurations. We therefore do not systematically explore retrieval variants such as query rewriting, hybrid search, or adaptive context selection, which could alter the observed retrieval ceilings. Finally, because we evaluate proprietary frontier and open-weight models through API access, results may vary as deployed systems evolve over time.

Ethics and Broader Impact

This work studies evidence grounding and provenance in long-context language models. Our benchmarks are constructed from synthetic or publicly available text and do not contain sensitive personal information. We do not train new foundation models; all experiments are conducted through inference-only evaluation of existing systems.

We believe evidence-based evaluation can improve transparency and verifiability in LLM-based systems by encouraging models to explicitly identify the context used to support their answers. Such capabilities may be particularly important in high-stakes applications such as legal analysis, scientific search, and medical document understanding, where unsupported or hallucinated answers can have significant consequences.

At the same time, citation generation should not be interpreted as a guarantee of faithful reasoning. A model may cite irrelevant or incomplete evidence while producing a plausible answer. We therefore view evidence-based generation as a complementary framework rather than a complete solution to factuality or interpretability in language models.
