Appendix A Prompt Templates

The haystack is line-numbered ([1], [2], …, [N]) and substituted into the haystack placeholder of each task template. We use four prompt variants: an answer-only variant (no system prompt), a Chain-of-Thought (CoT) variant (no system prompt), an evidence-based generation (EBG) variant that asks the model to cite supporting line numbers in JSON, and a CoT-based EBG variant (no system prompt) that requests both brief reasoning and the EBG JSON answer-and-evidence output.

Appendix B Additional Details of Synthetic Dataset

We provide additional details on the construction and structure of our synthetic dataset and present a representative example to illustrate the resulting task format and evidence organization.

B.1 Example

Consider facts “Himalaya Inc. launched FitBand” and “Himalaya Inc. is based in Mumbai”, with question “Which smart wearable was launched by a company based in Mumbai?” At L=10​KL{=}10\text{K} the two facts land at lines 56 and 67 among random distractors:

Neither line alone is sufficient: line 56 identifies the product but not the company location, while line 67 identifies the location but not the product. The model must therefore compose evidence across both lines. Under the EBG prompt template, the expected output is a JSON object containing both the answer and the cited line numbers:

Such a response is scored as correct on Ans, Evid, and Ans+Evid. The remaining nine needles follow the same structure with varied entities, relations, and answer forms.

Appendix C NoLiMa Datatset Adaptation Details

C.1 Needle settings

Table 2 presents the different needle templates used across different settings.

C.2 Single Needle (SN) setting

In this setting, 0402 and 0402Inv encode the same dietary fact about a character ({CHAR}) using different surface forms with altered word order. We refer to the first variant as the default form and the second as the inverse form. Similarly, needles 0405 and 0405Inv state that a character ({CHAR}) is vegan. These needles support both one-hop questions answerable directly from the needle (e.g., “Which character is lactose intolerant?”) and two-hop questions requiring an additional world-knowledge inference (e.g., “Which character cannot drink a cappuccino?”, which requires knowing that cappuccino contains milk). The SN context supplies the entity-specific primary needle but not the complete inference chain required by the question. For example, a needle stating that a character is vegan must be combined with parametric commonsense knowledge that veganism excludes eating fish.

We therefore refer to the cited primary needle in SN as anchor evidence. For SN, evidence accuracy measures whether the model cites the correct contextual anchor, and joint accuracy measures answer correctness together with anchor citation; these metrics should not be interpreted as establishing a complete context-only evidence chain. This distinction is specific to SN because part of the information required to answer the query may reside in the model’s parametric knowledge. Accordingly, SN citations cannot directly attribute the contribution of such internally stored information.

C.3 Two-needle (TN) setting

As shown in Table 2, we introduce two explicit secondary needles under the two-needle (TN) setting: TN-0402-S and TN-0405-S. These needles explicitly provide the world-knowledge fact required for two-hop reasoning (e.g., “CHAR said, ‘Cappuccino is a classic Italian coffee made with espresso and steamed milk.’,”). Each secondary needle pairs with the corresponding primary needles. For example, TN-0402-S pairs with 0402 and 0402Inv, while TN-0405-S pairs with 0405 and 0405Inv. Answering a two-hop question, therefore, requires retrieving and jointly reasoning over both the primary and secondary needles.

C.4 Contradictory Two-needle (CTN) setting

This setting introduces secondary needles that conflict with world knowledge. For example, CTN-0402-S claims that black coffee contains steamed milk, while CTN-0405-S claims that falafel contains minced lamb. As in TN, each secondary needle pairs with its primary needles (e.g., CTN-0402-S with 0402 and 0402Inv), testing whether models follow provided context or override it with parametric knowledge. For both question types, the primary needle provides an entity-specific anchor while inference requires unstated bridge knowledge. One-hop questions require a commonsense bridge (e.g., veganism implies avoiding fish), while two-hop questions require an item-composition bridge (e.g., Brandade is fish-based).

Appendix D Long-context EBG vs. RAG on MultiHop-RAG

This appendix analyzes an oracle-containing long-context (LC) reading condition and an open-corpus retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) condition on the MultiHop-RAG benchmark (Tang and Yang, 2024). The LC condition guarantees that every gold-evidence article is available to the reader together with 20 distractor articles, whereas the RAG condition must retrieve the required evidence from the full 609-article corpus. The purpose of this comparison is therefore to diagnose the contribution of open-corpus retrieval failures to end-to-end performance; it is not a pool-matched comparison of LC and RAG under identical candidate document sets. The motivation is direct: our synthetic two-hop benchmark and the NoLiMa-adapted benchmark are constructed haystacks, which leaves open the question of whether the trends we observe carry over to realistic, web-derived multi-document QA where RAG is the natural baseline.

The filtered MultiHop-RAG subset (§4.3) of 2,255 queries tests both EBG (line-level evidence) and RAG (chunked corpus). We run experiments on a 50-query pilot set, sampled with seed 0 and stratified across three types: ninf=13n_{\mathrm{inf}}{=}13, ncomp=21n_{\mathrm{comp}}{=}21, and ntemp=16n_{\mathrm{temp}}{=}16. We use the same queries, prompts, and scoring throughout, while LC and RAG differ in candidate-document pools as described below.

LC haystacks.

For each query, we assemble a mini-haystack of (i) all gold-evidence documents and (ii) 20 distractor documents sampled without replacement from the remaining corpus. Documents are randomly concatenated, split into sentence-level lines, and rendered in the lineno: text format used by our synthetic benchmark. Gold evidence facts are re-mapped to line numbers so EBG labels match the prompt. Mini-haystacks average ∼241\sim 241K characters (∼58\sim 58K tokens), within every model’s context window. This is the LC (full) condition.

RAG haystacks.

For each query, we construct RAG contexts at K∈4,10,25,50,100,200K\in{4,10,25,50,100,200}. The retriever searches the full 609-document corpus, divided into 256-token sliding windows (6,296 chunks). We embed chunks and queries with text-embedding-3-large, rank by cosine similarity, and use the top-KK chunks as the RAG context. Each chunk is prefixed with [CHUNK <rank> | <title>], and rendered with the same sentence-per-line numbering as LC. Gold evidence facts are re-mapped to lines in the retrieved context; unretrieved facts have no corresponding gold line.

The conditions are not pool-matched: LC has all gold source articles plus 20 distractors, whereas RAG must locate the required evidence across all 609 articles. This design deliberately preserves the native evidence-access setting of each approach in practice, enabling a realistic comparison between them under their respective retrieval assumptions.

D.1 Setup

Prompt modes.

Each (query, context) pair is evaluated under two prompts differing in one sentence:

  • •

    Answer-only (Ans∗\texttt{Ans}^{*}). The model returns a JSON object with only an answer field. We report Ans∗\texttt{Ans}^{*} accuracy.

  • •

    EBG. The model returns a JSON object with answer and lines fields. Scoring uses Ans (string match against the gold answer), Evid,(strict) (every gold line appears in the prediction), and Joint ≡\equiv Ans+Evid,(strict) (answer-and-evidence).

Both prompts share the same system message, instructions, and JSON example template, modulo the citation field. The system message and prompt templates are reproduced verbatim in our accompanying public code release for full reproducibility.

Models.

We evaluate three frontier LLMs whose context windows comfortably fit under the LC condition: GPT-5, Sonnet-4.5, and Gemini-3-Fl. All calls use temperature 0 (or provider equivalent), default sampling parameters, and parallel=5. This setup keeps decoding conditions consistent across models and experiments.

Scoring.

Ans matches the model’s answer string against the gold answer using the same normalization used in the synthetic and NoLiMa experiments. Evid (strict) requires the predicted line-id set to contain every gold line for that query; partial matches are scored separately as Evid (recall) but only Evid (strict) is used for Joint. API failures (timeouts, safety refusals, transient connection errors) are excluded from the denominator; in practice this affected at most one cell (Sonnet-4.5, RAG@200 EBG, n=49/50n{=}49/50). Thus, reported scores reflect successfully completed model calls only.

D.2 Experiment A: Long-context EBG on MultiHop-RAG

We run the LC condition to establish base rates and test RQ2 (Does requiring explicitly citing evidence improve answer accuracy?) on a non-synthetic benchmark. Each model sees the full mini-haystack (∼241\sim 241K characters) and is prompted in answer-only or EBG mode. Table 3 summarizes results.

Joint accuracy is much harder than Ans: under EBG, joint (Ans+Evid\textit{Ans}{+}\textit{Evid}) is only 28% (GPT-5), 8% (Sonnet-4.5), and 28% (Gemini-3-Flash). The gap Ans −- Joint ranges from 50 pp (Gemini) to 74 pp (Sonnet) and is concentrated on inference queries, mirroring the asymmetric retrieval finding from our synthetic two-needle setting: models routinely produce a correct answer while citing only one of the two required hops.

D.3 Experiment B: Retrieval analysis

Before running any LLM we measure how hard the retrieval problem itself is. For every query and every gold fact we record the rank of the first chunk that contains that fact; Hits@kk (all gold) counts the fraction of queries for which every gold fact appears in the top-kk. We compare two embedding models (text-embedding-3-small/large) and two chunkers (256-token sliding windows vs. sentence-level chunks); full results are in Table 4 (corpus-wide, N=2255N{=}2255), with our chosen configuration in bold.

The key qualitative finding is that retrieving at least one gold fact is easy (Hits@10 (any) =0.82=0.82 for our chosen config), but retrieving all gold facts is hard (Hits@10 (all) =0.19=0.19). Inference (multi-hop) queries are the most punishing: Hits@10 (all) is only 0.080.08 for that slice. For RAG to faithfully ground a multi-hop answer at k=10k{=}10, more than 90% of inference queries are doomed before the LLM is even called. This establishes a concrete retrieval ceiling on downstream RAG performance. Crucially, the bottleneck is not finding relevant evidence, but retrieving all pieces of evidence needed for a complete answer. Thus, many apparent reasoning failures downstream are already determined by missing context at retrieval time.

D.4 Experiment B′: Needle coverage on the pilot

For the 50 pilot queries, we repeat this analysis at every evaluated KK. Table 5 reports the fraction of queries with all gold facts (“needles”) retrieved in the top-KK and the fraction of individual gold facts appearing anywhere in the top-KK. These quantities upper-bound faithful joint accuracy and answer recall, respectively, for RAG on the pilot set.

D.5 Experiment C: Oracle-containing LC versus open-corpus RAG

The central experiment sweeps open-corpus RAG over six values of KK and compares it with oracle-containing LC under both prompt modes. All conditions use the same 50 queries, prompts, models, and scoring code, but differ in candidate-document pools: LC receives every gold-evidence article plus 20 distractors, whereas RAG searches the 609-article corpus. Table 6 thus measures the end-to-end cost of open-corpus retrieval relative to gold-source access, not a pool-matched comparison. The table tells three stories, one per metric.

Answer accuracy: oracle-containing LC exceeds open-corpus RAG under the evaluated budgets.

Across both prompts and all three models, oracle-containing LC outperforms open-corpus RAG for K≤100K\leq 100. At K=200K{=}200, with 96% gold-fact recall and 90% all-needles coverage, RAG ties LC for Sonnet-4.5 (68%68\%) but remains 4,pp below for GPT-5 (78%78\% vs. 82%82\%) and 10,pp below for Gemini-3-Flash (70%70\% vs. 80%80\%). At K=10K{=}10, the LC–RAG gap is 2222–4444,pp under answer-only prompting and 2626–3434,pp under EBG. These gaps include full-corpus retrieval and thus compare open-corpus RAG with evidence-guaranteed LC, not an intrinsic LC advantage under identical candidate pools.

Strict evidence: small-KK RAG and LC are comparable.

Evid (strict) is roughly flat across KK for each model (10–40% absolute), with no clean monotone trend. This reflects two distinct requirements for evidence correctness: all needles must be retrieved (coverage, Table 5) and the model must cite all of them correctly (citation behaviour). Small KK favors the latter because the citation surface is limited, whereas large KK favors the former as retrieval coverage improves. Increasing KK therefore trades easier citation selection for greater evidence availability, and these opposing effects roughly cancel. Consequently, small-KK RAG can remain comparable to LC on strict evidence despite substantially lower retrieval coverage.

Joint (faithful) accuracy: mixed.

Joint = Ans ∧\wedge Evid (also written as Ans+Evid) is the most diagnostic number. Two trends are visible. First, joint decreases with KK for every model: at large KK the citation surface grows, the model loses track of which retrieved chunk it used, and joint collapses despite the higher answer recall. Second, the best RAG joint is always at small KK (K=4K{=}4 for all three models), where the citation problem is trivial and the only queries that score are the ones whose needles happened to be in the top 4 (14% of queries). Aggregate joint therefore over-rewards a regime that only works on the easy fraction of queries. LC’s joint sits at 28%, 8%, 28% - competitive with RAG@4 for GPT-5 and Gemini, behind for Sonnet - and is computed over the full pilot set rather than the small subset where retrieval succeeded.

D.6 Discussion

We highlight four takeaways for the manuscript.

Takeaway 1: LC EBG dominates RAG for answer accuracy, at every realistic retrieval budget.

Under the answer-only prompt, the oracle-containing LC condition exceeds open-corpus RAG@10 by 2222–4444 pp and exceeds RAG@200 by 00–1010 pp. The same qualitative pattern holds under EBG. Because the two conditions do not share a candidate-document pool, these numbers quantify the combined cost of document discovery and passage retrieval relative to evidence-guaranteed reading; they are not a pool-matched estimate of an architecture-level LC–RAG effect.

Takeaway 2: RAG’s retrieval bottleneck is multi-hop coverage, not single-hop recall.

Hits@10 (any gold) is 82% but Hits@10 (all gold) is only 19% (Table 4); on inference queries the all-gold number falls to 8%. The principal source of the observed gap relative to the oracle-containing LC control is that, at small KK, open-corpus RAG rarely retrieves the complete union of annotated gold facts.

Takeaway 3: Citations as a reasoning scaffold replicate outside the synthetic setting.

Ans accuracy under EBG is higher than under the answer-only prompt for two of three models, with a striking +14+14 pp improvement for Sonnet-4.5 (Table 3). This is the RQ1 effect that was masked on our synthetic benchmark by ceiling performance.

Takeaway 4: The grounding gap is a real-data phenomenon.

The Ans −- Joint gap in the LC condition is 50–74 pp depending on model, and is largest on inference queries. Models routinely produce a correct multi-hop answer while citing only one of the two required hops  -  the same asymmetric-retrieval failure mode we documented on the synthetic benchmark, here observed on naturalistic web data.

D.7 Generalization to open-weight models

The preceding comparison uses three proprietary frontier LLMs. To test whether the observed pattern generalizes across model families, we repeat the same two evidence-access regimes, an oracle-containing LC condition and open-corpus RAG, with three open-weight models. To test whether the LC-EBG vs. RAG ordering is a property of the task rather than of a particular model family, we re-run the same conditions, using same mini-haystacks, same RAG contexts, same prompts and scoring code, with three open-weight models served through Fireworks.ai: GPT-OSS-120B, GLM-5.2, and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B (or Nemo-3.5-L in short). To obtain tighter estimates we scale this comparison to a larger stratified sample of n=200n{=}200 queries. We evaluate the two most informative RAG budgets, a realistic operating point (K=10K{=}10) and the near-saturation budget (K=200K{=}200, 90% all-needles coverage; Table 5), against the full LC condition. Table 7 reports the results.

The qualitative picture from Table 6 carries over. (i) Answer accuracy: oracle-containing LC exceeds the evaluated open-corpus RAG setup. At the realistic K=10K{=}10 operating point, LC’s Ans exceeds RAG@10 for all three models under both prompts: by +28+28 to +35+35 pp under the answer-only prompt and by +13+13 (GPT-OSS-120B), +36+36 (GLM-5.2), and +20+20 pp (Nemotron) under EBG - the same +26+26 to +34+34 pp EBG gap we observe for the frontier models. At the near-saturation budget K=200K{=}200 RAG closes some of the gap but overtakes LC for none of the three readers: LC Ans still leads by +2+2 (GPT-OSS-120B), +14.5+14.5 (GLM-5.2), and +19.7+19.7 pp (Nemotron), with the GPT-OSS-120B margin inside the bootstrap CI. The larger sample thus removes the one n=50n{=}50 anomaly (GPT-OSS-120B RAG@200 nominally above LC) and confirms LC≥\,\geq\,RAG@200 throughout. (ii) The grounding gap is model-agnostic. Under LC, the Ans−-Joint gap is 5252 (GPT-OSS-120B), 58.558.5 (GLM-5.2), and 42.742.7 pp (Nemotron) - the same 40–60 pp range as the frontier models. GPT-OSS-120B is the extreme case: it answers 54%54\% of queries correctly but achieves only 2%2\% joint accuracy, essentially never citing both required hops. (iii) Citation-as-scaffold is uneven for weaker readers. The Ans∗→{}^{*}\!\toAns (EBG) change on LC is +0.5+0.5 pp for GLM-5.2 but −21-21 pp for GPT-OSS-120B and −27-27 pp for Nemotron: the weakest open readers, unlike the frontier models, struggle to answer and cite simultaneously, so the citation requirement can hurt rather than help. Overall, the pattern that oracle-containing LC achieves higher answer accuracy than the evaluated open-corpus RAG pipeline at practical retrieval budgets, while retaining a substantial grounding gap, generalizes across proprietary and open-weight readers. This result continues to include the cost of full-corpus retrieval and is not a pool-matched comparison.

D.8 Limitations and next steps

The frontier-model experiments use a 50-query pilot, so the reported estimates remain subject to sampling variation, particularly for small question-type slices such as the 13 inference queries. Evaluating all 2,255 usable queries would provide tighter confidence intervals. We also hold the retriever fixed to text-embedding-3-large with 256-token sliding windows. Reranking, hybrid sparse–dense retrieval, query expansion, longer chunks, and document-aware indexing could improve the open-corpus RAG results. For the evaluated retriever, corpus-wide all-gold Hits@1010 is 19%19\% over the 2,255 usable queries; on the 50-query pilot, all-gold coverage at K=10K{=}10 is 28%28\%. Under the assumptions that the gold annotations are exhaustive and that every annotated fact is necessary, these coverage rates strongly constrain faithfully grounded performance at this retrieval budget.

A key design limitation is that the MultiHop-RAG LC and RAG conditions are not pool-matched. The LC condition is an oracle-containing reading control: every gold-evidence article is guaranteed to be present together with 20 distractor articles. The RAG condition instead performs open-corpus retrieval over the full 609-article corpus. Consequently, the reported LC–RAG gaps combine the effects of full-corpus document discovery, passage retrieval, and downstream reading; they should not be interpreted as an intrinsic ranking of LC and RAG under matched evidence access.

A complementary pool-matched RAG condition that retrieves from the same per-query gold-plus-20 candidate set would separate within-pool chunking and ranking effects from the cost of full-corpus document discovery. We leave this controlled comparison, together with evaluation of stronger retrieval pipelines and the full query set, to future work.

D.9 Reproducibility

All code, queries, and intermediate artifacts live under baselines/multihop_rag/ in the experiment repository:

  • •

    build_haystack.py: builds per-query mini-haystacks (LC condition).

  • •

    embed_and_rank.py: chunks the corpus, embeds, ranks gold facts; produces summary.json, fact_ranks.jsonl, and chunks.jsonl under retrieval_results/<config>/.

  • •

    build_rag_haystack.py: assembles per-KK RAG contexts from the retrieval artifacts.

  • •

    run_baseline.py: runs the LLM evaluation on either LC or RAG haystacks, supports --answer-only.

  • •

    aggregate_pilot.py, aggregate_rag_sweep.py: produce the tables above.

The 50-query pilot is reproducible with --seed 0 on processed/queries_d20.jsonl (built from the official MultiHop-RAG HuggingFace release of the corpus and queries).

Appendix E Long-context EBG vs. RAG on QASPER-MP

This appendix documents a second comparison of long-context evidence-based generation (LC EBG) against retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), this time on a multi-paper adaptation of QASPER (Dasigi et al., 2021) that we call QASPER-MP. Whereas MultiHop-RAG (Appendix D) tests multi-document reasoning on news, QASPER-MP tests it on scientific papers, where the gold question–answer–evidence triples were written assuming a single known paper. To make the task non-trivial under retrieval, we (i) place each gold paper alongside ten distractor papers, (ii) rewrite the question so it identifies the target paper by a realistic short reference (an author name or a 2–3 word topic cue), and (iii) evaluate in both LC and RAG conditions over the same 50-query stratified pilot.

The headline finding is that the aggregate score (Answer-F1 or LLM-judge, averaged over all questions) makes LC and RAG look roughly tied, but this tie hides an answerability asymmetry: LC EBG beats RAG by 5–22 judge points on answerable questions for every frontier model tested, while RAG “wins” on unanswerable questions because it over-refuses. The over-refusal mechanically matches the QASPER Unanswerable gold label on the 24% of pilot questions where that is the correct answer, pulling the aggregate up.

E.1 Setup

Dataset.

We use the QASPER dev split (N=1,005N=1{,}005 questions over 281 papers). Each question is annotated with an answer type (extractive, abstractive, boolean, or none - meaning unanswerable from the paper) and an evidence set: the list of paragraphs from the paper that support the answer. Up to three annotators contribute per question; we follow the official QASPER evaluator and take the max F1 across annotators.

50-query pilot.

We sample 50 questions, stratified by answer type, so that the composition matches the dev-split distribution: 13 boolean, 13 abstractive, 12 extractive, 12 unanswerable. This split (38 answerable, 12 unanswerable) is the denominator for every condition below.

Multi-paper haystacks (LC condition).

For each pilot query we build an 11-paper haystack consisting of the gold paper plus 10 distractor papers drawn uniformly from the dev split. Each paper is rendered with explicit document boundaries:

<paper>
<title>Paper title</title>
<abstract>Paper abstract</abstract>
<section>Section name</section>
Paragraph 1 of that section
Paragraph 2 of that section
…
</paper>

Lines are concatenated and numbered i: <line> so the model can cite specific lines as evidence (consistent with our EBG protocol). The median LC haystack size is ∼\sim32K characters; the largest is ∼\sim56K. The gold-evidence paragraph(s) for each query are re-mapped to line indices in the assembled haystack.

RAG condition.

We embed every QASPER dev paragraph and every (disambiguated) query with OpenAI text-embedding-3-large, and retrieve the top-KK paragraphs by cosine similarity. We evaluate four retrieval variants, factored as {flat,struct}×{pool11,full}\{\text{flat},\,\text{struct}\}\times\{\text{pool11},\,\text{full}\}:

flat_pool11.

Top-KK paragraphs retrieved from the same 11-paper pool as the LC haystack (pool-matched candidate corpus). The reader sees a flat list of retrieved paragraphs with a one-line [CHUNK <rank> | <title>] marker before each.

struct_pool11.

Same retrieval, but paragraphs are regrouped by their source paper and wrapped in the same XML layout used for LC. Within a paper, paragraphs are sorted by their original index, and discontinuities (gaps where intermediate paragraphs were not retrieved) are marked with a single ... line.

flat_full / struct_full.

Same as above but retrieving from the full dev corpus (N≈6,000N\approx 6{,}000 paragraphs) rather than the 11-paper pool. This is the realistic open-corpus RAG setting: the retriever must locate the target paper among hundreds of similar NLP papers using only the short cue in the rewritten question.

Models.

We evaluate five frontier reasoning models: GPT-5, GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.6, Claude Sonnet 4.5, and Gemini 3 Flash (preview). All runs use the same query set, the same retrieval indices, and the same EBG prompt template. Citation rules in the prompt forbid citing structural lines (<title>, <abstract>, <paper>, [CHUNK, or ...); these lines are present only as context.

Question disambiguation.

QASPER questions were written to be unambiguous given the paper; many become ambiguous in a multi-paper haystack (e.g., “What evaluation metrics were used?” becomes pathological with 11 candidate papers). We disambiguate each pilot question by inserting a short paper cue, chosen deterministically 50/50 from two cue types:

  • •

    Author cue (n=24n=24): “In Smith et al., …”, with surname(s) drawn from the arXiv metadata of the gold paper. Conventions: 1 author →\to “Smith”, 2 authors →\to “Smith and Doe”, ≥3\geq 3 authors →\to “Smith et al.”.

  • •

    Title cue (n=26n=26): “In the ⟨\langlecue⟩\rangle paper, …”, where the cue is a verbatim 2–3 word substring of the paper title (e.g., “Vietnamese Word Segmentation”, “Winograd Schemas”, “TF-IDF Features”).

Cues are intentionally short and realistic, matching what a researcher would type into a search box. This makes the retrieval problem genuinely harder than indexing on full titles or descriptive paraphrases.

E.2 Aggregate Performance: LC ≈\approx RAG (and why this is misleading)

Table 8 reports per-condition Answer-F1, Evidence-F1, and LLM-judge (an automated 0/0.5/1 grader using GPT-5; see Appendix E.5). Aggregating over all 50 pilot questions:

  • •

    LC and flat_pool11@3 are within ±\pm0.06 judge points for every model.

  • •

    struct_pool11@3 beats LC for GPT-5 and matches it for Gemini under the LLM judge.

On its face, this is the standard “LC is comparable to RAG” result.

The aggregate hides an answerability asymmetry.

Splitting the 50 queries into the 38 answerable and 12 unanswerable subsets tells a sharper story (Table 9).

Three observations:

  1. 1.

    LC EBG wins answerable questions cleanly. For all five models, LC has the highest Judge score on the 38-question answerable subset, with absolute gains over the best RAG variant of +0.05+0.05 (GPT-5), +0.13+0.13 (GPT-5.5), +0.13+0.13 (Opus-4.6), +0.08+0.08 (Sonnet-4.5), and +0.12+0.12 (Gemini-3-Flash). These gaps are robust to the citation-rule and discontinuity-marker changes described in Appendix E.4.

  2. 2.

    RAG over-refuses, and the refusals pay off on the unanswerable subset. flat_pool11@3 refuses 29–40% of answerable questions (vs. 16–18% for LC) because when retrieval misses the gold paragraph the reader sees only distractor content and sensibly says “Unanswerable.” Those same refusal-prone retrieval failures happen to be the right answer on unanswerable queries (where “Unanswerable” is gold), so RAG wins that subset by 0.17–0.25 judge points.

  3. 3.

    Realistic open-corpus retrieval makes LC win by a margin the aggregate cannot hide. The flat_full@10 row in Table 8 shows LC outperforming full-corpus RAG by 5–13 judge points on the aggregate already; the answerable-only gap is larger again (not shown). When the retriever must distinguish the gold paper from ∼\sim280 distractors using a 2–3 word cue, paper-level retrieval coverage drops to 48% (all-needles@10), and downstream answer quality follows.

The aggregate score thus rewards RAG’s high refusal rate. Once we condition on answerability, the LC >> RAG gap on actually answerable questions is consistent across models and retrieval variants.

E.3 Disambiguation Details and Cue Length Sensitivity

We initially experimented with longer “descriptive” cues generated by GPT-5 from each paper’s title and abstract (e.g., “In the cross-lingual zero-shot NMT paper”). These cues are unrealistically informative: they often include domain phrases that do not appear in the title at all, which makes retrieval implausibly easy. Embedding-based retrieval coverage with descriptive cues was 60.0% (all-needles@10, full corpus). Switching to the short, realistic cues described in Appendix E.1 dropped coverage to 48.0% - a 12-point hit - reflecting the fact that “In Smith et al.” or “In the BERTSUM paper” is a much weaker retrieval signal than a paraphrased domain summary.

We use the short, realistic cues throughout this appendix because they correspond to how researchers actually query systems in practice; the ++12pp coverage gain on descriptive cues would inflate RAG numbers relative to what users would experience.

E.4 Structured RAG, Citation Eligibility, and Discontinuity Markers

A first iteration of structured RAG produced a counterintuitive result: struct_pool11@3 underperformed flat_pool11@3 on Evidence-F1 across models (gaps of 0.07–0.12), despite carrying more information than the flat baseline (abstract per paper). On inspection, ∼\sim44% of structured-RAG citations pointed at <title> or <abstract> lines: when an abstract paraphrases the answer, the model cites it - but QASPER gold evidence excludes abstracts, so abstract citations cannot match gold.

We therefore made two changes to the structured layout and prompt used throughout the main results:

  1. 1.

    Citation eligibility. The EBG prompt forbids citing structural lines (<title>, <abstract>, <paper>, </paper>, [CHUNK, and ...). Models must cite at least one body paragraph line for any non-refusal answer. Titles and abstracts remain visible as context; they are simply not valid evidence.

  2. 2.

    Discontinuity markers. Within each paper, retrieved paragraphs are sorted by their original paragraph index, and any gap (the abstract followed by paragraph 2, or paragraph 5 followed by paragraph 9) is marked with a single ... line. This gives the reader explicit signal that some material is missing between the visible paragraphs.

Under this revised protocol (Table 8), structured RAG recovers: Evidence-F1 jumps by ++0.04 to ++0.15 per model and struct_pool11@3 beats or matches flat_pool11@3 for two of five models. The intuition that paper-level structure is useful is correct - it had been masked by a metric artifact.

E.5 LLM-Judge Evaluation

To control for token-F1 brittleness on paraphrases, we additionally score outputs with an LLM judge:

  • •

    Judge model: GPT-5.

  • •

    Inputs: the original question, all annotator gold answers, and the model prediction.

  • •

    Output: a single number in {0, 0.5, 1}\{0,\,0.5,\,1\}. The judge is instructed to be lenient about formatting and elaboration but strict about content; partial credit (0.5) is reserved for answers that capture some but not all required information. “Unanswerable” vs. “Unanswerable” scores 1.0; “Unanswerable” vs. a real answer (or the reverse) scores 0.0.

Judgments are cached by content hash so repeated scoring is free. Across all conditions, Judge scores are systematically higher than Answer-F1 (the judge is lenient about phrasing), but the ordering of conditions is preserved. The LC vs. RAG gap on answerable questions is larger under the judge than under Answer-F1, because the judge does not penalize Sonnet-4.5 and Gemini-3-Flash for their characteristic boolean elaborations.

E.6 Generalization to open-weight models

We repeat the QASPER-MP comparison with three open-weight models served through Fireworks.ai - GPT-OSS-120B, GLM-5.2, and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B - using the same retrieval indices, EBG prompt, and GPT-5 judge (Appendix E.5), scaled to a larger 200200-query stratified sample (n=150n{=}150 answerable, n=50n{=}50 unanswerable) for tighter estimates. Table 10 splits the results by answerability, exactly as Table 9 does for the frontier models.

The answerability asymmetry we documented for frontier models reproduces on every open-weight reader. LC EBG wins the answerable subset cleanly: the LC judge score is highest for all three models, beating the best RAG variant by +0.16+0.16 (GPT-OSS-120B), +0.24+0.24 (GLM-5.2), and +0.07+0.07 (Nemotron) - gaps as large as, or larger than, the +0.05+0.05 to +0.13+0.13 we observe for the frontier models. RAG over-refuses for the same mechanistic reason: flat_pool11@3 refuses 2121–33%33\% of answerable questions (vs. 77–12%12\% for LC), because a missed retrieval leaves the reader with only distractor content; those refusals then mechanically boost RAG on the unanswerable subset, where “Unanswerable” is gold. Realistic full-corpus retrieval widens the LC advantage: flat_full@10 answerable judge scores drop to 0.430.43–0.500.50, trailing LC by 0.090.09 to 0.240.24 judge points, as the retriever must find the gold paper among ∼\sim280 distractors from a 2–3 word cue. The open-weight results thus corroborate the central QASPER-MP finding: once conditioned on answerability, long-context EBG beats every RAG variant, and the aggregate “tie” is an artifact of RAG’s refusal behavior.

E.7 Strengthening RAG: metadata-in-chunk retrieval

The full-corpus RAG deficit above is partly a retrieval failure rather than solely a limitation of the downstream reader. After v2 disambiguation, each query carries only a short, typically 22–33 word cue identifying the relevant paper. In the baseline index, however, candidate chunks are embedded as raw paragraph text, without any explicit representation of document identity. The retriever must therefore infer the connection between a sparse paper-level cue in the query and a paragraph whose local content may never mention the paper title or otherwise reveal its source. This mismatch is especially consequential in the full-corpus setting, where evidence from the gold paper competes with paragraphs drawn from the entire ∼\sim281-paper dev corpus. Even when the query contains enough information to identify the intended document, the embedding space has no direct document-level feature with which to exploit that signal, making it easy for the gold paper - and consequently the relevant evidence within it - to fall outside the retrieval budget.

A natural way to give RAG a fairer chance is therefore to expose document identity directly to the retriever by injecting metadata into the indexed chunks. We rebuild the retrieval index so that every paragraph is embedded together with its source paper’s title, using the representation “title\n\nparagraph”. This modification creates an explicit lexical and semantic bridge between the short paper cue supplied by v2 disambiguation and every paragraph originating from that paper, while preserving the paragraph text needed to rank evidence within the document. We then re-run the hardest retrieval condition, flat_full@10, at n=200n{=}200 for all five readers. Importantly, this intervention is confined to retrieval: generation-side rendering, prompting, context construction, and reader settings are unchanged. Thus, any downstream improvement can be attributed to changing the representation used for ranking rather than to providing the reader with additional metadata or altering the generation procedure.

Metadata-in-chunk produces a large improvement in evidence retrieval. On the 200200-query set, the fraction of queries for which the full gold-evidence set is recovered within the top-1010 increases from 43.5%43.5\% to 61.0%61.0\%, a gain of 17.517.5 percentage points. Gold-paragraph recall rises even more substantially in relative terms, from 30.6%30.6\% to 50.3%50.3\% (+19.7+19.7 pp). These gains indicate that the original full-corpus deficit was not simply caused by an insufficient top-kk budget: a substantial portion arose because the retriever lacked a representation of the very document-level signal introduced during query disambiguation. Prepending the title allows that signal to influence ranking directly, increasing both the probability that the correct paper is represented among the retrieved chunks and the amount of gold evidence that reaches the reader.

The retrieval gains propagate consistently to answer quality (Table 11). On the answerable subset, the judge score improves for every model. The four strongest readers - GPT-5, Sonnet-4.5, GPT-OSS-120B, and GLM-5.2 - gain between +0.10+0.10 and +0.13+0.13, while Nemotron improves by +0.03+0.03. The answerable-question refusal rate also falls by 55–88,pp, consistent with fewer queries reaching the reader with distractor or insufficient context. That the same retrieval-only intervention benefits readers with different capabilities strengthens the interpretation that evidence availability is a shared bottleneck across otherwise diverse reader architectures and levels of baseline answer quality. Part of the reader-level degradation under full-corpus RAG is therefore upstream: when document identity is represented during retrieval, more evidence survives the top-1010 bottleneck, giving all five readers a better opportunity to answer. This shows that chunk representation can materially affect end-to-end RAG performance over a large, heterogeneous corpus.

Crucially, a stronger retriever narrows but does not close the LC gap. With metadata-in-chunk, flat_full@10 trails LC on the answerable subset for all models - by 0.040.04 (Sonnet-4.5), 0.060.06 (Nemotron), 0.080.08 (GPT-OSS-120B), 0.140.14 (GLM-5.2), and 0.150.15 (GPT-5) judge points. Roughly half the full-corpus LC advantage is recoverable by fixing retrieval, but a residual remains: even when the right paragraphs are retrieved, removing document context costs answer quality relative to reading the full neighborhood. This points beyond evidence discovery: retrieval preserves passages but discards surrounding structure. That context supplies definitions, antecedents, methodological details, and cross-paragraph relationships needed to interpret evidence. The central finding remains robust to better RAG - LC EBG still wins.

E.8 Summary

QASPER-MP corroborates the picture in Appendix D: under the pool-matched pool11 condition, long-context EBG and RAG end up at comparable aggregate scores, but the mechanism is asymmetric. RAG’s higher refusal rate inflates its score on unanswerable questions; on the answerable subset - where retrieval quality actually matters - LC EBG beats every RAG variant for every one of the five frontier models we tested. The gap is largest for the strongest readers (Opus-4.6 and GPT-5.5 each show +0.13+0.13 judge points LC over best RAG on answerable questions), suggesting that LC EBG benefits disproportionately from stronger long-context comprehension. The gap widens further when the retrieval corpus expands from the apples-to-apples 11-paper pool to the realistic full-corpus setting, where LC outperforms the best RAG configuration by 5–13 judge points.

Appendix F Long-context EBG: Synthetic and NoLiMa-based Datasets

This appendix collects the controlled long-context EBG results that support RQ2–RQ4: the synthetic two-hop benchmark (§ F.1) and the NoLiMa-based benchmark (§ F.2).

F.1 Ans-only vs EBG on Synthetic Dataset

Observations.

Fig. 4 compares evidence-based generation (EBG) against answer-only prompting on the synthetic two-hop benchmark, highlighting both the advantages and limitations of requiring explicit evidence attribution.

  • •

    Performance rapidly saturates for all frontier models. Across nearly the entire 10K–1M character range, all models operate close to ceiling performance, with accuracies clustering near 100% under both prompt settings. This indicates that the synthetic two-hop benchmark is largely solved by current frontier systems once the relevant evidence is successfully retrieved, and that increasing context length alone does not substantially reduce answer accuracy for the strongest models.

  • •

    Answer-only and EBG prompting achieve nearly identical performance across all context lengths. For GPT-5 and Gemini-3-Fl, Ans∗ (answer-only prompting) and Ans (answer with evidence prompting) remain effectively indistinguishable from 10K to 1M characters, with almost all cells at or near 100% accuracy. The difference heatmap confirms that the vast majority of entries have zero difference, indicating that adding citation requirements does not materially affect answer correctness on this synthetic benchmark.

F.2 Ans-only vs EBG on NoLiMa-based Dataset

Observations.

As shown in Table 12, EBG prompting is more beneficial for multi-hop queries than for simple one-hop queries. In one-hop settings, many strong models already perform near ceiling under answer-only prompting, leaving little room for explicit evidence organization to help. In some cases, the additional structure introduced by EBG even hurts performance, suggesting that it may interfere with models that already perform strong implicit retrieval or that are sensitive to extra reasoning overhead. The benefits of EBG become clearer in the two-hop setting, where models must retrieve and combine evidence across multiple pieces of context. The best long-context performers are GPT-5 and Gemini-3-Fl, but for different reasons. GPT-5 is highly robust regardless of prompting strategy, while Gemini-3-Fl gains substantially from EBG in two-hop settings.

The strongest evidence in favor of EBG comes from the Gemini-3-Fl two-hop results, where EBG improves performance consistently across almost all context lengths, including the 1M setting. The Sonnet models also show frequent gains from EBG in two-hop tasks, further supporting the view that explicit evidence organization is most useful when reasoning requires multiple retrieval steps. In contrast, the strongest evidence against universal EBG use comes from GPT-4o, where EBG substantially lowers performance in both one-hop and two-hop tasks.

Overall, the table suggests that EBG is especially valuable for long-context multi-hop reasoning in models, but it may be unnecessary for simple one-hop retrieval.

F.3 Strict EBG on NoLiMa-based Dataset

Observations.

Fig. 5 reports the combined Ans+Evid accuracy across models, context lengths, and reasoning types. Since this metric requires both the final answer and the supporting evidence to be correct, it is a stricter measure than answer accuracy alone. The results show clear differences in how well models remain both accurate and grounded as context length increases.

One-hop performance.

In the one-hop setting, the reported joint Ans+Evid metric measures answer correctness together with citation of the primary contextual anchor, rather than a complete context-only reasoning chain, because for one-hop, part of the inference relies on bridge knowledge not stated in the haystack (such as veganism implying avoidance of fish or lactose intolerance implying avoidance of milk. Here, we observe that most frontier models perform very strongly at short and medium context lengths. GPT-5, Sonnet-4, Sonnet-4.5, Gemini-2.5-Fl, and Gemini-3-Fl frequently achieve near-perfect or perfect accuracy across many context lengths. This suggests that when only one relevant piece of evidence needs to be retrieved, strong long-context models can usually identify the evidence and produce the correct answer reliably.

Gemini-3-Fl is the strongest one-hop model overall, maintaining 100% accuracy across all evaluated context lengths, including 1M characters. GPT-5 is also highly robust, achieving 100% accuracy across most context lengths and only dropping slightly to 94% at 1M. Gemini-2.5-Fl also remains strong, although it declines at longer contexts, reaching 81% at 600K and 700K before recovering to 94% at 1M.

GPT-4.1 performs well in one-hop reasoning, but its performance decreases at the largest context length, reaching 81% at 1M. GPT-4o and o3-mini show much weaker robustness. GPT-4o drops substantially after 100K characters, while o3-mini degrades sharply beyond 200K characters, falling to 31% at 500K and 19% at 700K.

Two-hop performance.

The two-hop setting is significantly harder. Even models that perform very well in one-hop reasoning show larger performance drops when they must retrieve and combine multiple pieces of evidence. This indicates that long-context multi-hop reasoning requires more than simply locating one relevant span; the model must maintain multiple pieces of information and reason over their relationship.

Gemini-3-Fl is the strongest model in the two-hop setting. It maintains high accuracy across the context range and achieves 93% at 1M characters. GPT-5 is strong from 10K to 700K, but drops to 81% at 1M. GPT-4.1 performs well through mid-range contexts but declines at 1M, reaching 62%.

F.4 TN vs. CTN on NoLiMa-based Dataset: Adherence to Contextual Evidence

We conduct an experiment on the NoLiMa-based dataset to evaluate whether LLMs remain faithful to contextual evidence in two-hop reasoning questions when presented with either factual secondary evidence that aligns with world knowledge (TN) or counterfactual secondary evidence that conflicts with world knowledge (CTN; e.g., “black coffee has milk”).

Experiment.

Under TN and CTN, each query is associated with two needles. We insert the primary needle at the middle of the haystack (depth 0.50.5) and the secondary needle at one of the sampled depths {0.0,0.33,0.67,1.0}\{0.0,0.33,0.67,1.0\}. Since questions must be answered strictly from the provided context, success in CTN requires relying on the contradictory contextual evidence rather than parametric memory. We evaluate the performance of TN and CTN using Ans and Ans+Evid accuracy metrics.

Observations.
  • •

    Contradiction reliably hurts performance. Averaged across models, CTN reduces Ans accuracy by ≈\approx7.0 pp (76.2% →\to 69.2%) and Ans+Evid by ≈\approx5.9 pp (49.9% →\to 44.0%).

  • •

    The Ans+Evid accuracy metric is much harder than Ans. Ans+Evid is far below Ans in both TN and CTN, indicating many correct-answer cases still fail to produce a complete evidence trail.

  • •

    Robustness varies sharply by model. Gemini-3-Fl and GPT-5 remain most stable; the largest Ans+Evid drops under CTN occur for GPT-4.1 (≈\approx-13 pp), Gemini-2.5-Fl (≈\approx-10 pp), and o3-mini (≈\approx-8.6 pp).

  • •

    Depth sensitivity persists under contradiction, with the CTN penalty tending to be larger when the secondary needle is deeper, consistent with degraded multi-evidence retrieval under harder placements, i.e., mostly at depths 0.33 and 0.67.

  • •

    CTN remains below TN across context lengths, indicating contradiction amplifies long-context brittleness as both conditions degrade with length.

  • •

    Contradiction weakens evidence grounding, not just answers. CTN lowers citation rates for both needles (primary ≈\approx-7.4 pp and secondary ≈\approx-4.6 pp), pointing to provenance failure as a primary failure mode under conflicting information.

  • •

    The answer dimension degrades too, but less than the joint metric. Figure 6 reports Ans accuracy for the same runs. Every model except Gemini-3-Fl loses answer accuracy under contradiction, with the largest drops for GPT-OSS-120B (≈\approx-17 pp), Sonnet-4.5 (≈\approx-16 pp), and Gemini-2.5-Fl and Sonnet-4 (≈\approx-12 pp each).

F.5 EBG vs. CoT Prompting on NoLiMa-based Dataset

Experiment.

We compare answer accuracy under standard EBG and CoT prompting separately for one-hop and two-hop questions. We define Δ=Ans−Ansc\Delta=\texttt{Ans}-\texttt{Ans}^{c}, where Ans denotes answer accuracy under EBG prompting and Ansc\texttt{Ans}^{c} denotes answer accuracy under CoT prompting. Positive values of Δ\Delta therefore indicate an advantage for EBG, whereas negative values indicate an advantage for CoT.

Observations.

As shown in Fig. 7(a), the effect of CoT is substantially larger for two-hop questions than for one-hop questions. On a model-macro average, CoT improves answer accuracy by approximately 8.58.5 pp for one-hop questions and 27.227.2 pp for two-hop questions. At the model level, CoT never reduces aggregate one-hop accuracy: it improves accuracy for eight models and matches EBG for GPT-5 and Gemini-3-Fl. The largest one-hop gains occur for GPT-OSS-120B (+23.6+23.6 pp), GPT-4o (+20.0+20.0 pp), and o3-mini (+19.3+19.3 pp).

For two-hop questions, CoT achieves higher aggregate answer accuracy for every evaluated model. The improvements range from 5.95.9 pp for GPT-5 to 68.868.8 pp for GPT-OSS-120B, with large gains also observed for GLM-5.2 (+42.3+42.3 pp), o3-mini (+33.3+33.3 pp), Gemini-2.5-Fl (+31.3+31.3 pp), and GPT-4o (+30.8+30.8 pp). This larger two-hop effect suggests that explicitly eliciting a short reasoning step is particularly useful when answering requires an additional inference beyond direct needle retrieval. Because vanilla CoT also removes the citation and JSON-output requirements, however, this comparison should be interpreted as a comparison between complete prompting strategies rather than as an isolated estimate of the effect of reasoning alone.

F.6 EBG vs. CoT-EBG Prompting on NoLiMa-based Dataset

Setup.

To examine whether explicit reasoning remains beneficial when evidence citation is retained, we compare standard EBG with CoT-EBG. We report Ans so that this comparison is directly commensurable with the vanilla-CoT comparison in Appendix F.5, which can only be scored on answer accuracy because the plain CoT prompt requests no citations. Holding the metric fixed across the two experiments isolates the effect of the citation requirement itself. We define Δ=Ans−Ansc​e\Delta=\texttt{Ans}-\texttt{Ans}^{ce}, where c​ece denotes CoT-EBG; negative values therefore favor CoT-EBG.

Observations.

Fig. 7(b) shows a smaller and more model-dependent effect for one-hop questions. CoT-EBG improves aggregate answer accuracy for five models, matches EBG for two, and lowers it for three, with a model-macro average of 2.22.2 pp in favor of CoT-EBG. This mixed result is consistent with the near-ceiling performance of several models on direct one-hop retrieval, where an additional reasoning instruction has limited room to help and may introduce unnecessary output complexity. The two-hop result is more consistent: CoT-EBG improves aggregate Ans accuracy for every evaluated model, by 12.312.3 pp on a model-macro average. The gains range from 2.42.4 pp for GPT-4.1 to 25.525.5 pp for Gemini-2.5-Fl. Substantial improvements are also observed for GPT-OSS-120B and GLM-5.2 (+23.6+23.6 pp each), o3-mini (+12.0+12.0 pp), and Gemini-3-Fl (+10.4+10.4 pp). Thus, explicitly eliciting a brief reasoning step remains beneficial when the evidence-citation requirement and output schema are retained, particularly for multi-hop questions.

Taken together, the two experiments suggest that the gains from structured prompting are not attributable to citation formatting alone. Explicit reasoning improves answer accuracy both under vanilla CoT and when the EBG citation requirement is retained, with the largest and most consistent effects appearing in the two-hop setting.

Appendix G RAG on NoLiMa-based Dataset

We use text-embedding-3-small to generate embeddings for both the NoLiMa haystack lines (with inserted needles) and the corresponding queries, and perform retrieval using cosine similarity.

G.1 Retrieval Analysis

Table 13 summarizes how the retrieval requirements of a RAG system changes as the haystack context length grows from 10​K10\mathrm{K} to 1​M1\mathrm{M}. The first row reports the average number of vectors, or indexed chunks, produced from the full context. As expected, this number increases with context length: for example, the retriever searches over only 6666 vectors at 10​K10\mathrm{K} context, but over 5,7305{,}730 vectors at 1​M1\mathrm{M} context.

The remaining rows measure the retrieval depth required for full-coverage. Here, full coverage means that the retrieved top-kk set contains all evidence facts needed to answer every query. Thus, the reported number of vectors is the smallest value of kk such that no required evidence is missed.

For one-hop queries, where the answer depends on a single evidence fact, the required retrieval depth grows moderately with context length. At 10​K10\mathrm{K} context, retrieving only 22 vectors, corresponding to 350350 characters, is sufficient for full coverage. However, at 1​M1\mathrm{M} context, full coverage requires retrieving 9696 vectors, corresponding to 22,91022{,}910 characters. This shows that even relatively simple queries require a larger retrieval budget as the haystack becomes longer.

For two-hop queries, where the answer depends on combining multiple evidence facts, the retrieval requirement grows much more sharply. At 10​K10\mathrm{K} context, full coverage requires retrieving 1010 vectors, or 1,9561{,}956 characters. At 1​M1\mathrm{M} context, however, it requires retrieving 890890 vectors, or 202,412202{,}412 characters. This indicates that multi-hop evidence is substantially harder to retrieve in long-context settings, since the relevant pieces of information may be distributed across many more chunks.

Several observations follow from these results. First, the total number of indexed vectors grows approximately linearly with context length, increasing from 6666 vectors at 10​K10\mathrm{K} to 5,7305{,}730 vectors at 1​M1\mathrm{M}. Second, the retrieval depth required for full coverage is much smaller than the total number of indexed vectors, but it still grows substantially as the context becomes longer. Third, two-hop queries are consistently more demanding than one-hop queries: at 1​M1\mathrm{M} context, two-hop full coverage requires 890890 vectors, compared with only 9696 vectors for one-hop full coverage. This is more than a 9×9\times increase in the number of retrieved vectors:

89096≈9.27.\frac{890}{96}\approx 9.27.

Fourth, the retrieved character budget also grows significantly. At 1​M1\mathrm{M} context, one-hop full coverage requires 22,91022{,}910 characters, whereas two-hop full coverage requires 202,412202{,}412 characters. Thus, two-hop retrieval requires nearly nine times more retrieved text:

202,41222,910≈8.83.\frac{202{,}412}{22{,}910}\approx 8.83.

Another important observation is that standard small retrieval budgets, such as top-55 or top-1010, are unlikely to provide full coverage in long-context settings. For instance, at 100​K100\mathrm{K} context, one-hop full coverage already requires top-1010, while two-hop full coverage requires top-9292. At 1​M1\mathrm{M} context, the required two-hop retrieval depth increases to top-890890, which is far beyond typical RAG configurations.

Overall, the table shows that standard small top-kk retrieval settings may be insufficient for long-context RAG, especially for multi-hop queries. While one-hop retrieval remains relatively manageable, two-hop retrieval at 1​M1\mathrm{M} context requires retrieving a large fraction of the indexed chunks:

8905730≈15.5%.\frac{890}{5730}\approx 15.5\%.

Therefore, as context length increases, guaranteeing full evidence coverage can require a very large retrieved character budget, reducing the efficiency advantage usually associated with RAG.

G.2 Character and Pronoun Sensitivity in Needle Retrieval

Motivation.

During retrieval analysis, we observed that the 0405 needle family requires substantially larger top-kk budgets to achieve reliable retrieval compared to the 0402 family (Figure 8). This suggests that retrieval difficulty may be influenced not only by reasoning complexity but also by the surface form of the needle itself. The default 0405 template contains a gendered pronoun:

“Then {CHAR} mentioned that he has been vegan for years.”

Because the pronoun he is independent of the inserted character name, it may introduce additional semantic signals in the embedding representation that are not directly relevant to the query.

Character sensitivity analysis.

To investigate this effect, we compute cosine similarity between the query embedding and needle sentences instantiated with different character names drawn from the NoLiMa corpus. Figure 9 shows the top retrieved variants of the needle and their similarity scores for the query “Which character cannot eat Brandade?”.

Although the sentence semantics remain unchanged, we observe noticeable variation in similarity scores across character substitutions. This indicates that character tokens themselves influence the embedding representation and can affect retrieval ranking.

Effect of pronoun removal.

To isolate the role of the gendered pronoun, we construct a rephrased variant of the needle (0405-R, Table 2) that removes the pronoun while preserving the meaning:

“Then {CHAR} mentioned being vegan for years.”

We recompute similarity scores for both the original and rephrased needles across multiple character substitutions. Figure 10 compares cosine similarity between the two formulations.

Across most characters, the rephrased template yields slightly higher similarity scores. While the improvement is modest for individual instances, it is systematic across characters, suggesting that removing the pronoun reduces semantic noise in the embedding space.

Implications for RAG retrieval.

These results help explain the higher retrieval budget required for the 0405 needle family observed earlier. When the needle contains additional syntactic elements that are not directly aligned with the query semantics, embedding similarity becomes less discriminative. In large haystacks, even small similarity differences can significantly affect ranking, pushing the correct needle lower in the retrieval list and increasing the required top-kk budget.

G.3 Retrieval Analysis under Embedding, BM25, and Reranker-RAG Pipelines

Motivated by the results and observations in Table 13, we further investigate whether the observed retrieval bottleneck is specific to embedding-based semantic retrieval or persists across alternative retrieval and ranking strategies.

Setup of Embedding-RAG.

We first consider the embedding-based RAG pipeline from the preceding experiment (§ 5.1.3), restricting the evaluation to Book 1 (B1cB^{c}_{1}). The pipeline follows the same retrieval setup as before: the haystack is divided into chunks, represented using dense vector embeddings, and ranked by semantic similarity to the query. We retain the original chunking, retrieval, and full-coverage evaluation protocol, and report the minimum top-kk required to retrieve all evidence for one-hop and two-hop queries, together with the corresponding retrieved character budget. Thus, the Embedding-RAG results in Table 14 serve as the semantic-retrieval baseline against which Okapi BM25 and Qwen3-Reranker-8B are compared.

Setup of BM25-RAG.

To examine whether the retrieval limitations observed with embedding-based RAG are specific to semantic similarity search, we replace the vector embedding-based retriever with Okapi BM2522 2 https://pypi.org/project/rank-bm25/, a lexical retrieval method based on term matching and term-frequency statistics. We keep the evaluation protocol unchanged and measure the minimum retrieval depth required to achieve full evidence coverage for both one-hop and two-hop queries across increasing NoLiMa context lengths. As in our primary analysis, full coverage is defined as the smallest top-kk for which all required evidence facts are present in the retrieved set for every sample. We report both this retrieval depth and its corresponding character budget in Table 14.

Setup of Reranker-based RAG.

We further evaluate whether a stronger learned ranking stage can reduce the retrieval depth required for complete evidence coverage. Specifically, we use Qwen3-Reranker-8B, a fine-tuned reranking model, to reorder candidate passages (retrieved by the embedding-based RAG retriever) according to their relevance to the query. We then evaluate the resulting ranking using the same full-coverage criterion as the BM25-RAG and Embedding-RAG settings. This experiment tests the extent to which a learned reranker can move required evidence toward the top of the ranking and consequently reduce the context passed to the downstream model.

Observations.

We observe that BM25-RAG consistently requires substantially larger retrieval budgets than Embedding-RAG, with the difference becoming more pronounced as context length increases. At 1M characters, full coverage of one-hop queries requires 307 vectors (102,475 characters) with BM25-RAG, compared with 104 vectors (23,589 characters) for Embedding-RAG. The same pattern holds for two-hop queries, where BM25-RAG requires 1,061 vectors (265,785 characters), compared with 920 vectors (217,152 characters) for Embedding-RAG. Thus, replacing semantic retrieval with Okapi BM25 does not remove the full-coverage bottleneck; instead, lexical retrieval generally requires retrieving more of the haystack to guarantee that all necessary evidence is available. This gap suggests that semantic similarity provides a stronger ranking signal for isolating relevant evidence as the distractor pool expands. Moreover, the persistent two-hop overhead across both retrievers indicates that jointly recovering multiple evidence pieces remains intrinsically more demanding than single-evidence retrieval.

As shown in Table 14, Qwen3-Reranker-8B improves retrieval efficiency over BM25-RAG and Embedding-RAG. For one-hop queries, evidence ranks first across all context lengths, yielding full coverage at top-11 with 62 characters. For two-hop queries, depth grows with context length: at 1M characters, Reranker-RAG reaches full coverage with 149 vectors (21,372 characters), compared with 920 vectors (217,152 characters) for Embedding-RAG and 1,061 vectors (265,785 characters) for BM25-RAG. Thus, a fine-tuned reranker dramatically reduces the retrieval budget for full evidence coverage. Nevertheless, increasing top-kk for two-hop queries shows that stronger reranking does not eliminate the difficulty of jointly surfacing evidence as the haystack grows. The one-hop–two-hop contrast suggests that evidence multiplicity, not context length alone, drives the remaining burden: joint coverage becomes harder when multiple passages must survive the cutoff.

G.4 Randomly Sampled Haystacks vs. Top-kk Ranked Retrieval

Setup.

We examine whether LLMs answer more accurately when we give them a randomly sampled long-context haystack or a compact context formed by top-kk ranked retrieval. In the long-context setting, we provide the model with the Book 1 haystack at a target character length and insert the needle at predefined depths. This setting corresponds to randomly sampled haystacks: the long-context construction procedure embeds the relevant evidence within a larger context and determines the surrounding distractors and needle positions. In contrast, the retrieval setting replaces the full randomly sampled haystack with a retrieval-ranked context. For each query, we compute cosine similarity between the query embedding and each chunk embedding in the corresponding vector database, rank all chunks by similarity score, and select the minimum top-kk prefix that contains all gold needle evidence for that condition. We call this value the best top-kk.

Because long-context and retrieval inputs differ substantially in structure, we compare them under approximately matched character budgets rather than matched nominal context labels. For each Book 1 haystack, we first compute the total character count of the best top-kk retrieved chunks. We then select the long-context condition whose haystack character count most closely matches that retrieval character count. For example, the best top-kk retrieved context for the 1M-character haystack contains 217,152 characters; we therefore compare this retrieval condition against the 200K-character long-context condition, since the two inputs match most closely in character budget. Throughout, “context length” denotes character count rather than token count.

We use the same answer+evidence prompt as the long-context EBG setting, constructed from the selected top-kk chunks and gold evidence metadata. Models produce an answer with cited evidence. We denote retrieval and matched long-context answer accuracy as AnsRAG\mathrm{Ans}_{\mathrm{RAG}} and AnsLC\mathrm{Ans}_{\mathrm{LC}}, respectively. The primary comparison is the accuracy delta:

Δ=AnsRAG−AnsLC.\Delta=\mathrm{Ans}_{\mathrm{RAG}}-\mathrm{Ans}_{\mathrm{LC}}.

A positive value means that top-kk ranked retrieval outperforms randomly sampled long-context prompting under the matched character budget, while a negative value means that randomly sampled long-context prompting outperforms top-kk ranked retrieval.

Table 15 summarizes the character-budget matching procedure. The table reports, for each original Book 1 haystack length, the best top-kk value, the character count of the corresponding retrieved context, and the matched long-context character budget we use for comparison.

Figure 11 reports retrieval answer accuracy under the answer+evidence prompt, and Figure 12 reports the resulting Δ\Delta difference values across models and matched context lengths.

Observations.

Figure 12 shows that the relative advantage of top-kk ranked retrieval versus randomly sampled long-context prompting depends strongly on the model. Since each cell reports Δ=AnsRAG−AnsLC\Delta=\mathrm{Ans}_{\mathrm{RAG}}-\mathrm{Ans}_{\mathrm{LC}}, positive values indicate that the top-kk retrieved context performs better, whereas negative values indicate that the randomly sampled long-context haystack performs better.

Overall, top-kk ranked retrieval competes strongly with long-context prompting under the matched character-budget setting. For GPT-4o, retrieval outperforms long-context prompting in four of the five matched budgets: 50K (+31+31 pp), 70K (+22+22 pp), 100K (+28+28 pp), and 200K (+9+9 pp). GPT-4o therefore benefits substantially when we replace the larger randomly sampled haystack with a compact retrieval-ranked context. GPT-5 also shows near parity between the two settings, with deltas close to zero across all budgets (+3+3, 00, +3+3, +6+6, and 00 pp). For GPT-5, once the retrieved top-kk context contains the relevant evidence, the additional surrounding haystack context provides little or no answer-accuracy benefit.

In contrast, GPT-4.1 consistently favors the randomly sampled long-context haystack. Its deltas remain negative at every matched budget, ranging from −9-9 pp at 100K to −34-34 pp at 90K. GPT-4.1 therefore exploits information from the broader haystack context more effectively than from the compact top-kk context, even when the retrieved context contains the necessary gold evidence. The Claude models show a similar but weaker long-context preference. Sonnet-4 improves under long-context prompting at 50K, 70K, 90K, and 100K, with the largest gain at 90K (−31-31 pp), but retrieval performs slightly better at 200K (+6+6 pp). Sonnet-4.5 also favors long-context prompting at most matched budgets, especially 90K (−25-25 pp) and 100K (−16-16 pp), while matching retrieval at 50K and showing only a small long-context advantage at 200K (−6-6 pp). O3-mini swings unpredictably across budgets in both directions: long-context prompting helps at 50K (−12-12 pp), retrieval helps at 70K and 200K (+12+12 pp and +9+9 pp), and the two settings tie at 90K and 100K.

A notable pattern emerges at the 90K budget, which favors long-context prompting most strongly. Four models show large negative deltas: GPT-4o (−25-25,pp), GPT-4.1 (−34-34,pp), Sonnet-4 (−31-31,pp), and Sonnet-4.5 (−25-25,pp). Evidence completeness therefore does not guarantee retrieval superiority. Even when the top-kk context contains the required needles, the model may benefit from broader discourse, surrounding distractors, or positional structure of the original haystack. Retrieval can therefore alter the contextual relationships through which evidence is interpreted, making compression effectiveness model-dependent. Conversely, strong positive deltas for GPT-4o and near-zero deltas for GPT-5 show that compact retrieval removes distractor burden without hurting accuracy for some models.

Overall, the results do not support a single universal winner between randomly sampled haystacks and top-kk ranked retrieval. They instead reveal a model-specific tradeoff. Top-kk retrieval outperforms long-context prompting when compact evidence-focused contexts help the model avoid distraction, as GPT-4o demonstrates most clearly. Long-context prompting outperforms retrieval when models benefit from the broader haystack context, as GPT-4.1 and the Claude models demonstrate. GPT-5 emerges as the most retrieval-robust model in this comparison, showing that a sufficiently strong model answers equally well from the compact retrieved context and the matched randomly sampled haystack.

G.5 Embedding-RAG vs Reranker-RAG under EBG Prompting

The preceding retrieval analysis (Table 14) shows that Qwen3-Reranker-8B can rank required evidence substantially closer to the top of the retrieved context than embedding-based similarity search. However, improved retrieval ranking does not necessarily translate into better end-to-end generation: even when the same evidence is available, its position within the retrieved context may affect a model’s ability to identify, reason over, and correctly attribute that evidence. Motivated by this distinction, we evaluate whether the retrieval-order improvements from reranking translate into higher joint Ans+Evid accuracy when the amount of retrieved context is held fixed.

Setup.

We compare Embedding-RAG and Reranker-FixedTopk-RAG across four LLMs. For each LC-matched budget in Table 15, Embedding-RAG retrieves full-coverage top-kk chunks by cosine similarity. Reranker-RAG uses the same chunks and preserves the top-kk and character budget, but re-orders them using Qwen3-Reranker-8B relevance scores. No chunks are added or removed; the pipelines differ only in evidence ordering. This comparison isolates whether placing relevant evidence earlier improves generation rather than conflating ranking quality with context volume. With evidence availability and context size fixed, differences can be attributed to ranking and reveal whether models benefit from prioritizing relevant chunks. We evaluate both pipelines with our EBG prompt over n=8n=8 examples, comprising four needles under one-hop and two-hop queries. Results appear in Table 16.

Observations.

Table 16 shows that reranking improves end-to-end answer accuracy over embedding-based retrieval, with gains particularly pronounced at larger context budgets. Sonnet-4.5 benefits consistently from reranking, reaching 100% accuracy from 50K–100K and retaining an advantage at 200K. GPT-OSS-120B exhibits the largest gain at longer contexts, improving from 62.5% to 100% at 100K and from 50% to 87.5% at 200K. GPT-4.1 and GLM-5.2 also improve in most settings, although reranking is not uniformly beneficial: GPT-4.1 drops from 87.5% to 75% at 100K, while GLM-5.2 drops from 62.5% to 50% at 50K and remains unchanged at 90K.

Overall, across the 20 model–budget combinations, Reranker-RAG improves over Embedding-RAG in 15 cases, ties in three, and underperforms in only two, indicating that improved evidence ordering can translate into better downstream answer generation even when the retrieved context budget is fixed. The larger gains at higher budgets suggest that retrieval quality remains important even when more context is available, particularly as irrelevant passages increasingly compete for the reader’s attention. Because both pipelines contain identical chunks, these gains isolate ordering rather than evidence availability, suggesting that readers are sensitive to where relevant evidence appears within the retrieved context.

Appendix H Dataset Source and Statistics

Table 17 summarizes all datasets used in this work along with their sources and licenses. We construct or adapt all datasets from publicly available sources. We construct the synthetic two-hop haystack entirely using iterative LLM prompting for distractor generation and manually curated needles, and we release it under CC BY 4.0. The NoLiMa-based dataset adapts the haystack construction procedure and needle set from Modarressi et al. (2025), which is released under the Adobe Research License. We use MultiHop-RAG (Tang and Yang, 2024) as released under the ODC-By license, and re-map gold evidence facts to line-level labels for EBG evaluation. We derive QASPER-MP from the QASPER dev split (Dasigi et al., 2021), released under CC BY 4.0, and extend it to a multi-paper setting by pairing each gold paper with ten distractor papers and rewriting questions with short realistic paper cues.

Appendix I Model Information

We evaluate ten proprietary frontier and three open-weight models via their APIs. Table 18 lists each model along with its provider, source URL, and license. All models were queried at temperature 0 (or the provider-equivalent default) with no additional fine-tuning or adaptation.

Appendix J Artifact Use and Intended Use

We use all existing datasets and models consistently with their intended use. MultiHop-RAG, QASPER, and NoLiMa are used strictly for research evaluation, consistent with their release conditions. All proprietary models are accessed via official APIs in accordance with provider terms of service. All derived datasets introduced in this work are intended exclusively for research use and do not conflict with the access conditions of the original artifacts.
